interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: Foundation Models Meet Agriculture: Challenges Beyond Pretraining
papers.authors: Vishal Nedungadi , Xingguo Xiong , Marc Rußwurm , Ioannis N. Athanasiadis
papers.abstract: Global food security and sustainable climate action increasingly rely on robust, scalable agricultural monitoring. Earth observation foundation models have emerged as powerful, label-efficient tools across general remote sensing domains, yet early attempts to deploy them for agricultural applications have yielded surprisingly poor results. We hypothesize that this performance gap stems from the extreme heterogeneity of agricultural landscapes and the inherent inability of current earth observation foundation models to adapt to task-specific nuances. In this work, we systematically evaluate two critical bottlenecks hindering the deployment of foundation models in agricultural tasks, benchmarking two earth observation foundation models, a foundation model designed for tabular data, and conventional supervised baselines across seven real-world agricultural datasets spanning yield prediction, phenology estimation, and crop classification. First, we identify a pretraining-deployment modality gap: agricultural downstream tasks frequently require diverse, non-imagery data modalities that earth observation foundation models are architecturally unequipped to ingest, while a foundation model built for tabular data handles this heterogeneity more naturally. Second, we formalize the agricultural task space across five structural axes to demonstrate why current models fail to generalize reliably, resulting in highly unstable model rankings across evaluation settings. By characterizing these structural and modal gaps, our insights highlight the friction between general-purpose architectures and specialized agricultural downstream data, providing a strategic roadmap for developing the next generation of domain-aware foundation models.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly relevant to foundation models for Earth observation and tabular data, with insights on modality gaps that apply to astronomical surveys. The discussion of task-specific adaptation is useful for JWST data.
papers.Short digest: This paper investigates why Earth observation foundation models underperform in agricultural tasks, identifying a pretraining-deployment modality gap. The main claim is that these models struggle with non-imagery data modalities and task-specific nuances, leading to unstable rankings. For astronomy, this highlights the need for multimodal foundation models that handle catalogs, spectra, and images together, as in JWST analysis. A concrete workflow could be evaluating foundation models on galaxy classification using both images and photometric catalogs. The paper's caveat is that it focuses on agriculture, but the structural analysis transfers to astronomy.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the modality gap analysis applies to astronomical data types like spectra and photometric tables.
Look for the five structural axes that define task space, to see if they map to astronomical tasks.
Verify the performance of tabular foundation models on heterogeneous data, which is relevant for multi-wavelength catalogs.

papers.title: DS-Lighting: Making Agent Harnesses Explicit for Data-Science Automation
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown promise for automating data-science workflows, yet their end-to-end performance depends critically on the agent harness that represents tasks, manages execution state, constrains output artifacts, and provides evaluation feedback. Existing data-science agents often leave this harness implicit, making results difficult to reproduce, compare, and attribute across heterogeneous tasks. We introduce DS-Lighting, a unified harness toolkit that makes harness design explicit for data-science automation. DS-Lighting decomposes the harness into four reusable layers: data, workflow, execution, and evaluation, and represents diverse agents as executable operator programs that support both predefined pipelines and adaptive search. We further integrate multiple open-source data-science benchmarks into an MLE-Bench-style task format, enabling controlled comparison under a shared task interface, sandboxed runtime, and metric protocol. Experiments across agents, harnesses, models, and ablations show that explicit harness design improves reproducibility, comparability, and reliability, while reducing avoidable system-level failures in end-to-end data-science workflows. Our code is available at this https URL
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses LLM agents for data-science automation, which is relevant to automated scientific discovery and research workflows. The explicit harness design could transfer to astronomical data analysis pipelines.
papers.Short digest: The paper tackles the problem that LLM agents for data-science tasks often have implicit, poorly reproducible harnesses. It introduces DS-Lighting, a toolkit that decomposes the harness into data, workflow, execution, and evaluation layers, representing agents as executable operator programs. This matters for astronomy because it could provide a structured way to build reproducible, comparable AI-driven analysis pipelines for large survey data. A concrete workflow could be using DS-Lighting to automate SED fitting or source classification across JWST catalogs. However, the paper focuses on generic data-science benchmarks, so I should check whether the harness supports domain-specific tools and data formats used in astronomy.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the harness supports custom data loaders or domain-specific file formats (e.g., FITS).
Look for examples of adaptive search or predefined pipelines that could be adapted to iterative fitting tasks.
Assess whether the evaluation layer can incorporate domain-specific metrics like photometric redshift accuracy.

papers.title: CoVA-SFT: A Large-Scale Dataset for Chain of Visual Abstractions
papers.authors: Tsung-Han Wu , Heekyung Lee , Anya Ji , Haoming Chen , Trevor Darrell , Joseph E. Gonzalez , David M. Chan
papers.subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has dramatically improved large language models (LLMs) by allowing them to decompose problems into intermediate steps. While CoT is widely effective for linguistic tasks, text-only CoT forces models to serialize visual problems into awkward prose. Although architectural solutions exist to process visual inputs, the community lacks a massive, multi-step, self-corrected dataset to teach models how to build and maintain internal visual workspaces when solving purely textual reasoning problems. To address this limitation, we introduce CoVA-SFT, a highly structured corpus of 51.9K samples containing over 222K multimodal reasoning steps across 5 distinct layout families and 17 complex tasks, and CoVA-Bench, a companion benchmark of 1,700 held-out test samples spanning the same tasks for reproducible evaluation. By providing explicit rationale formulations, agentic renderings, and verification loops, CoVA-SFT teaches multimodal language models to interleave text and visual abstractions. We validate the dataset by demonstrating that models fine-tuned on CoVA-SFT outperform all interleaved CoT baselines by more than 2x on average on CoVA-Bench, though they still fall short of strong text-only CoT baselines, highlighting open challenges for future work.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper introduces a dataset for chain of visual abstractions, which is relevant to multimodal models that combine text and visual reasoning, potentially useful for astronomical image analysis.
papers.Short digest: The paper presents CoVA-SFT, a large-scale dataset for teaching multimodal language models to interleave text and visual abstractions in reasoning. It includes 51.9K samples with multimodal reasoning steps. This is relevant because it could inform the development of LMMs that reason over astronomical images and spectra, combining visual and textual information.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the dataset includes any scientific or astronomical visual reasoning tasks.
Look for details on how the visual abstractions are generated and whether they could be adapted to astronomical data.

papers.title: Towards a Systems Foundation for Agentic Skills: Architecture, Lifecycle, and Security
papers.authors: Sanket Badhe , Deep Shah , Priyanka Tiwari , Nehal Kathrotia
papers.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
papers.abstract: Autonomous large language model (LLM) agents increasingly face reliability, context consumption, and execution stability bottlenecks when deployed on complex, long-horizon tasks. While monolithic prompt engineering and stateless tool-calling paradigms struggle to scale, the field is rapidly converging toward \emph{agentic skills}: modular procedural abstractions that externalize execution knowledge into reusable, executable, and portable artifacts. This paper establishes a unified systems foundation and reference architecture for the agentic skills ecosystem. We formalize skills as externalized procedural knowledge bridging high-level cognitive planning with deterministic execution environments, and systematically delineate the architecture across a nine-stage lifecycle: autonomous discovery, authoring and representation formats, memory storage, dynamic retrieval and routing, composition and orchestration, execution and repair, lifelong adaptation, empirical evaluation, and security governance. We further examine marketplace dynamics, public registries, and emerging adversarial threat vectors, alongside runtime verification and defense mechanisms. Finally, we categorize system implementations across software engineering, operating system navigation, embodied robotics, and scientific discovery, while highlighting critical open challenges in continual learning and benchmark realism. This work establishes agentic skills as a foundational paradigm for building scalable, robust, and verifiable autonomous language agents.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly relevant to LLM agents for scientific discovery, covering architecture and lifecycle of agentic skills, which could apply to astronomy workflows.
papers.Short digest: The paper establishes a systems foundation for agentic skills, which are modular procedural abstractions for LLM agents. It covers a nine-stage lifecycle including discovery, authoring, retrieval, and execution, and discusses applications in scientific discovery. This matters for astronomy because it provides a framework for building reusable, robust agents for data analysis and literature review. One could imagine using it to create agents for JWST data reduction or source classification. However, the paper is a position paper with no concrete implementation, so it requires further work to apply. Check for specific examples in scientific discovery and how skills are evaluated.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for concrete case studies in astronomy or physics.
Check if the lifecycle stages are actionable for building astronomical agents.
Assess the security and verification mechanisms for reliable scientific use.

papers.title: Agent Zero Memory: Provenance-Aware Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents need durable, faithful memory of everything a user or organization has said and stored, yet most memory systems commit to a single organizing structure (a fact store, a vector index, or a knowledge graph) and inherit its blind spots. We present Agent Zero Memory, a provenance-aware long-term memory system that distils a user's conversations, files, and connected sources into three parallel memory systems, each capturing a different facet of the same history: an episodic Memory Events timeline that makes when and what changed first-class, an associative entity-event knowledge graph that links people and projects across sessions, and a semantic, curated, citation-locked Hierarchical Documentary Memory (HDM) of durable facts. A retrieval turn runs an intent gate (so self-contained turns add no latency), a source router, and three concurrent agentic searches, one per system, each a tool-using loop over hybrid (embedding + lexical) search under agent-controlled filters; their grounded, cited answers are integrated into one answer with a single confidence. We formalize the reading discipline: every learned item is a provenanced item carrying its origin, timestamp, and evidence pointer, and every answer is read under a citation lock, so it may cite only evidence its reader actually opened; fabrication is structurally excluded and the system abstains rather than guesses. On two public benchmarks the system sets a new state of the art: 95.60% on LongMemEval and 93.60% on LoCoMo, improving over the strongest prior systems by +0.73 and +1.10 points. A controlled study across eight backbone LLMs characterizes the accuracy-cost-latency frontier: accuracy varies by only 3.4 points while per-query cost varies by ~30x, with near-state-of-the-art quality at up to 20x lower cost per query, the signature of memory-driven, rather than model-driven, quality.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses long-term memory for LLM agents, which is relevant to building research agents for astronomy that need to accumulate knowledge across papers and datasets. The provenance-aware design aligns with reproducible scientific workflows.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of LLM agents lacking durable, faithful memory of past interactions and stored information. It proposes a memory system with three parallel components—episodic timeline, knowledge graph, and curated document memory—each with citations to source evidence. For astronomy, this could help an agent remember findings from JWST papers and link them to specific datasets or analyses. I could imagine using it to build a research assistant that tracks literature, data products, and analysis steps across a long project. However, it is benchmarked on general conversational tasks, so I should check if the memory structures scale to scientific documents and multi-modal data.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the memory system handles multi-modal data (images, spectra) or only text
Look for evaluation on long-horizon scientific tasks or only general benchmarks
See if the citation-locking mechanism prevents hallucinated references in scientific contexts
